V. LePan, former assistant under secretary of state for external affairs, Mr. A. F. W. Plumptre, who was assistant deputy minister of finance for international affairs, and Mr. Escott Reid, who has long been associated with the Department of External Affairs and was formerly high commissioner to India and Canadian ambassador to Germany.
The statement they have issued, Mr. Speaker, points out that although the primary objective of the government of the United States may have been the maintenance of freedom and self determination, they are convinced that this objective cannot now be reached by the means that are being employed. They ask-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was trying to remind the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs of the nature of the request that has been made. May I sum it up by saying they are asking that the Canadian government take a lead in soliciting other countries to make an appeal for a cease fire in Viet Nam in the hope that this will be the first step-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman should ask his question.

speechtext:
I want to ask the Prime Minister or Secretary of State for External Affairs what reply is being made to this request, and whether the Canadian government is prepared seriously to undertake a solicitation of other governments who may be interested in an attempt to bring an end to the war in Viet Nam.

June 27. 1967
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR CANADIAN ACTION TO EFFECT CEASE FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I may even take as long to answer this question as the hon. gentleman took to ask it. I have received the communication, Mr. Speaker; as a matter of fact I received it this morning. Indeed, I have already talked to Mr. Escott Reid about it, as he happened to be in Ottawa today.
As my hon. friend knows, the communication welcomes the government's efforts to promote a peaceful settlement in Viet Nam and is intended to reinforce these efforts. As I understand the proposals Mr. Speaker, they take for their starting point the need for negotiations on a cease fire and a peaceful settlement. To bring this about they look to a cessation of the bombing of North Viet Nam coupled, if that were possible, with the cessation of infiltration by North Viet Nam and a cessation of the build-up of the forces of South Viet Nam's allies.
These proposals do not in any way conflict with government thinking. We have always made it clear that we wanted to see the bombing stopped, but that we also wanted to see, the infiltration stopped and negotiations started. I should remind the house, however, that proposals very much like these were made by President Johnson in his message of February 7 to President Ho Chi Minh. They were turned down by President Ho Chi Minh oh February 15, on the familiar ground that an unconditional cessation of the bombing and all other acts of war against North Viet Nam would have to precede any talks between the two sides.
I want to assure the hon. member and the house that the government is not losing sight of the need to set in train the process of negotiation in Viet Nam. Nor will the house need to be reminded of the key importance which the government attaches to a halt in the bombing in paving the way for such negotiation. This will be clear from the proposal we advanced on April 11 and which we still see as offering a valid approach to a reversal of the course of events in Viet Nam.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR CANADIAN ACTION TO EFFECT CEASE FIRE
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Considering that the statement of the three gentlemen in question differs from President Johnson's proposal in that it suggests an unconditional cessation of the bombing, and that the United States should express the hope that the North Vietnamese will stop its military build up in return for the assurance that the United States and its allies will act similarly, is the government of Canada prepared to give the lead to other

countries which are also interested in trying to get a group of countries in the world to support a declaration asking for an unconditional cessation of the bombing in the hope that negotiations and a peaceful settlement will follow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR CANADIAN ACTION TO EFFECT CEASE FIRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have already, I think, indicated our position in this matter, most recently at the North Atlantic Treaty Organization council meeting a few weeks ago. I would, however, point out to my hon. friend that even an unconditional cessation of bombing has now been linked by the authorities of North Viet Nam, in certain of their more recent statements, with the withdrawal of United States forces as well, before negotiations can begin. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall not continue to have this escalation in demands on the side of the north.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR CANADIAN ACTION TO EFFECT CEASE FIRE
speechtext: I have a related question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who has relied heavily on the international control commission for information from South Viet Nam. Can the minister tell us whether that commission is likely to produce a report in the near future, as it has not made a formal report for two years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR CANADIAN ACTION TO EFFECT CEASE FIRE
speechtext: I do not expect that in the foreseeable future there will be a report by the commission that will be unanimously concurred in.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-REQUEST FOR CANADIAN ACTION TO EFFECT CEASE FIRE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RESIDENCE REQUIREMENTS, APPEAL COURT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that neither the minister nor I had an opportunity the other day to make any statement about this bill, and in view of the complaints of some members in this regard, I should like the permission of the committee to make a short statement.
My remarks on the introduction of this bill need not be very long because the amendments proposed to the Citizenship Act are of a kind with which I am confident we can all agree, and which in our centennial year seem to me, at any rate, to be especially appropriate. Basically they are designed to remove grounds of discrimination which exist between natural born and other Canadians; to relax the language requirements for applicants who because of their age have difficulty in learning a new language; to provide flexibility in the requirements concerning residence in Canada before a person applies for citizenship, and to provide for a citizenship appeal court. In addition there are a number of amendments of a technical nature relating to persons of Newfoundland origin and with regard to procedures, the regulation-making power and the penalty provisions.
June 27, 1967

Canadian Citizenship Act
With regard to the matter of discrimination, I am recommending that the provision in the act whereby other than natural born Canadians lose their citizenship on residence for ten years or more outside of Canada be eliminated.
Several members, I am sure, have come across cases of people who have been granted citizenship, who live outside of Canada for good and sufficient reasons, and who suddenly find they have lost their citizenship. While it has been possible to allow them to resume their status, the confusion, the problems and even hardship which this provision has created seem to me quite unnecessary, and the provision has been discriminatory. Also on the point of discrimination, natural born citizens are not liable to loss of citizenship by reason of failure to return to Canada to face charges of treason under the Criminal Code or offences under the Official Secrets Act. This amendment will place other than natural born Canadians on the same footing in this connection as their fellow citizens who have natural born status.
Having regard to residence, under the act as it now stands an applicant must have "acquired Canadian domicile" and have resided in Canada for one year immediately preceding the date of his application. Canadian domicile is defined by reference to the Immigration Act, and means that a person acquires Canadian domicile when he has his place of domicile in Canada for at least five years after having landed in Canada.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The amendments the bill is suggesting will do away with this concept as a requirement for becoming a citizen. In its place there will be a requirement that a person must be a landed immigrant and have resided in Canada for five out of the eight years prior to his application. Generally speaking, this means immigrants will be eligible for citizenship five years after landing. However, we are proposing an important additional change by providing that a person who has resided in Canada before becoming a landed immigrant may count half that period toward the residence required after being landed. There will also be provided an additional element of flexibility in that the requirement of residence for one year immediately prior to application will be changed to a period of 12 months in the 18 months before application.
Amongst the requirements on which an applicant for citizenship must satisfy a court is that of language. He must have an adequate
[Mr. Bechard.l
knowledge of either of our official languages or, if not, have resided continuously in Canada for more than 20 years. The courts have been reasonable in the interpretation of this provision and generally speaking they consider persons qualified in this respect if their knowledge of one of our languages is adequate to their particular circumstances whatever they may be. Nevertheless there are cases particularly of older people, who find it quite difficult to learn one of our languages and they cannot therefore satisfy a court on this point. They do not have to if they have resided in Canada for 20 years. This bill recommends that the period be reduced to ten years in the case of a person who immigrated to Canada at the age of 40 or over. We are also proposing that the language requirement be waived if an applicant is the spouse, widow or widower of a Canadian citizen.
Suggestions have been made from time to time that when a person's application for citizenship has been refused by a court there should be an opportunity for him to appeal to a higher court to prove that he does possess the required qualifications and is a fit and proper person to be granted citizenship. While there have been only a few such cases in recent years, the government nevertheless agrees with this view. Accordingly, we are proposing the establishment of a citizenship appeal court consisting of a judge of the exchequer court to hear appeals from negative decisions of citizenship courts. The citizenship appeal court will be a court of record and will, as I have indicated, be empowered to hear and determine all appeals from final decisions of courts that an applicant is not a fit and proper person to be granted citizenship. It will also be empowered to hear appeals at any place in the country.
I should note at this point that the discretion to grant citizenship will still remain with the minister. Citizenship has always been a privilege bestowed by a country, and not a right of the person who seeks it. Let me say at once, however, that we are very glad to have persons become citizens of this country, to do what we can to facilitate in every possible way the granting of citizenship to those who apply and are qualified for it, and particularly to ensure that those who apply are heard fairly and their eases considered carefully.
The remaining provisions of the bill are of a technical nature and relate largely to procedures on which explanation, if members wish it, will be dealt with in committee where we now are. I should perhaps mention one matter
June 27, 1S67

of special interest to Newfoundlanders. After Newfoundland came into confederation the Canadian Citizenship Act was changed with the intention that the full terms of the act be extended to Newfoundland in accordance with the terms of union. However, despite the fact that the authorities at the time thought they were extending the complete terms of the act to cover people of Newfoundland origin, doubt was raised that this intention was in fact carried out. We are therefore including amendments in this bill which we are assured by the lawyers will indeed make certain that the complete provisions of the citizenship act cover people of Newfoundland origin.
The minister has not long had the responsibility for the administration of the citizenship act, but one thing she has discovered since she has had this responsibility is that it is an extremely complex law of a rather esoteric nature. The amendments we are recommending will result in considerable improvements, but we must remember it is 20 years since the law was first put on the statute books and it has been amended from time to time to fill gaps. Therefore, if the house approves this measure the minister will ask her officials to stand back and take a searching look at our citizenship concepts as embodied in the act and regulations, and as they have come down from previous naturalization laws, with a view to seeing whether the whole scheme should be revised to meet modern circumstances and conditions. Because this is a com-lex subject and because the status and rights of individuals are involved, we doubt that this can be done quickly, but the minister intends to spur the project on.
Mr. Chairman, I wish at this moment to try to reply to questions asked by hon. members the last time we studied this bill in committee. The hon. member for Royal dealt with the registration of births abroad; he was concerned about that matter. I dealt with this problem when a private member's bill introduced by the hon. member for Carleton was studied by the house. I wish only to emphasize at this point that registration not only serves a useful administrative purpose but it is also very much in the interest of the person himself. Such registration provides clear evidence to that person that he is a Canadian. It assists him to enter Canada easily and it enables him to identify himself in the future to Canadian authorities abroad should he ever need to do so. From the administrative point of view, it quickly enables a Canadian official to identify a person who is a Canadian and
Canadian Citizenship Act thus perform any services which are requested of him.
This is not to say that the present system is perfect and might not be improved. However, there are implications for other departments as well as this one and these would have to be taken into account in proposing any changes. I can assure the hon. member that this matter will be reviewed promptly.
The hon. member for Royal also dealt with the matter of the revision and consolidation of regulations. The minister and the department recognize the validity of the point made that the regulations need revision and tidying up. We are giving priority to this task and hope to have results in the relatively near future.
With regard to the humanitarian interpretation of the act, which matter was also raised by the hon. member for Royal, I agree with him in this respect and the minister proposes to bring to the attention of the courts the remarks made on the matter in this debate.
Several hon. members referred to booklets which have been published for the instruction of new citizens. These booklets are not produced, by the way, in the citizenship registration branch but in the citizenship branch of the department. A number of them are made available to prospective citizens when they call at the court offices. We are glad to have hon. members' views on them. Perhaps I should say that the booklets seem to appeal to a significant portion of the public, because aside from the free distribution to newcomers they are offered for sale at a nominal cost of from 35 cents to 50 cents by the Queen's printer and have consistently rated high on the Queen's printer's best seller list.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
With regard to the guide to Canadian citizenship which was specifically mentioned, I should emphasize that a judge may ask any questions he likes when examining an applicant. This booklet is, as it says, only a guide. It was produced several years ago and I believe the time has arrived when consideration should be given to whether any booklet at all is required or if the text of the existing one should be substantially revised. In any event,
I want to assure hon. members that we will be glad to reconsider and review the whole matter and undertake to do so.
The hon. member for Norfolk referred specifically to the new booklet for the use of
1994	COMMONS
Canadian Citizenship Act immigrants. This is to be a presentation booklet to people who have recently become Canadians. I am glad to say this booklet has been completed and has been distributed either yesterday or today.
The suggestion was made by the hon. member tor Oxford that a booklet should be prepared on the operations of parliament, which seems to me to be a good suggestion. It may be that some work in this area has already been done in the Speaker's office. In any event, I intend to ask the officials of the department to study this possibility.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, our centennial of confederation is but five days away. How fitting and appropriate, therefore, it is that this afternoon we should be discussing Canadian citizenship. I had hoped that the proposals of the government in the citizenship bill would have been imaginative and vigorous, a genuine call to arms for the Canadian nation. Instead, this afternoon what we have before us rather than a full revision of the Canadian Citizenship Act is a patchwork bill, a most pedestrian measure. It is an ad hoc bill, an improvisation in every particular. I suggest that by this timorous and uncertain legislation the Secretary of State has lost a tremendous opportunity to speak out for Canada on the eve of the centennial. Missed opportunities are seldom recaptured. I regret especially the failure of the government to seize this special opportunity to express our pride in Canadian citizenship.
The parliamentary secretary has laboured hard this afternoon to clothe this bill with a distinction it assuredly does not possess. Today it is hardly fashionable to talk of citizenship or nationality. Allegedly sophisticated people do not believe in it. I am sufficiently old fashioned, sir, to have great pride in nationality and in citizenship. I like the words which the Minister of Transport used in his address at Memorial University on May 19, 1967. I put them aside for just such an occasion, and although I would rarely quote the Minister of Transport I want to do so on this occasion:
In many quarters today, pride of nationality is no longer fashionable. Nationalism is called an evil thing. There are many who say, and perhaps more who think, we should cast aside all local or national ties and become "citizens of the world". I agree with those who say that the only hope for humanity is that all or most of the inhabitants of the globe should learn to be citizens of the world, with a sense of responsibility to all their fellow human beings. But I do not believe that to become a good citizen of the world, one has to give up narrower loyalties. No one seriously argues that the world
[Mr. Bechard.l
DEBATES	June 27, 1967
would be a better place if all men and women lost their distinctive individual personalities and became indistinguishable one from another. Nationality is nothing more than the collective personality of a group of people. I am convinced that collective personalities, both national and local, are just as essential to human happiness and a good life as individual personalities. In my view, nationalism, which is the sense of common nationality, is harmful only when it is directed to harmful ends like the promotion of racial hatred and aggression against other nations.
I believe these are wise words from the Minister of Transport. They reflect completely my view of citizenship and nationality. I believe they are totally in character with the first speech from the throne delivered in this parliament by Lord Monck on November 7, 1867. I want to take a moment to read the second paragraph of that speech from the throne:
I congratulate you on the legislative sanction which has been given by the Imperial Parliament to the Act of Union, under the provisions of which we are now assembled and which has laid the foundation of a new nationality, that I trust and believe will, ere long, extend its bounds from the Atlantic to the Pacific ocean.
Who wrote those words, "a new nationality"? Those were the words of Thomas D'Arcy McGee. They were adopted by Sir John A. Macdonald and they were put in the first speech from the throne. Those words were approved by the first cabinet, a cabinet which consisted of many of the fathers of confederation, the architects of this nation. They were men of French heritage, of Scotch, Irish and English heritage. What they said, and what they sought for this nation, was a new nationality, a nationality not French, not Anglo-Saxon, not Scotch, not Irish, not Welsh and not of any other old land, but one which bore proudly and uniquely the name "Canadian".
This is the approach I take to this bill and that is where I think the deficiency of this bill lies, that on the eve of confederation there is not the inspiration in the bill that is needed in these particular circumstances. I confess to some of my friends who are of other national backgrounds than mine that what irritates me most is that French speaking Canadians lump me in as Anglo-Saxon when my heritage is Irish and my people were Irish rebels long before the French ever stirred from the sleep of medievalism.
If I may use the words of Frank Underhill, the new nationality was to "include and transcend the two groups of English speaking and French speaking Canadians." I believe a reiteration of some of the words Underhill used
June 27, 1967

in the Massey Lectures of 1963 on "The Image of Confederation" would be useful at this time:
The experiment of the new nationality that they thus proclaimed was of a nationality that should link together a variety of rather isolated, little colonial communities scattered across the northern half of the continent, and that, in particular, should include and transcend the two groups of English speaking and French speaking Canadians, divided though they were in race, language, and religion.
I underline the words "include and transcend".
That is, it was a complex nationality; and they were well aware of their own boldness in the initiation of this experiment.
This, sir, is the type of boldness I wish we had demonstrated in this bill this afternoon. I wish it really represented a leap forward into that new nationality contemplated and forecast in the first speech from the throne.
I should like to congratulate the officials of the department upon the new booklet which was d.stributed yesterday to members of parliament and which is to be distributed to new citizens hereafter. I believe it is an excellent production. I think it is exceedingly worth while. I believe it will give that feeling of unity which all new citizens should have, that feeling of belonging which is so important to someone who has just taken the oath of allegiance.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I hope that when these presentations are made, judges of the citizenship court will fully appreciate the responsibilities which are theirs. I have spoken of this before in the house, and the hon. member for Royal spoke of it the other day. I do not think there are any officials in our country who have a heavier responsibility to display human, warm understanding of the problems of the people who are before them than the citizenship court judges. They can and ought to convey a real welcome to those who have done our country the honour of accepting our citizenship, we having given them the privilege of being citizens of this nation.
I have heard many complaints about a very few of the judges of the citizenship court. There is one citizenship court the judge of which I should have fired when I was minister of citizenship and immigration, and I still say he should be fired. In this locality this man is doing damage to the whole image of Canadian citizenship, and I hope he can either be properly disciplined or else his services
Canadian Citizenship Act properly dispensed with by the governor in council.
The parliamentary secretary said that this bill had four purposes. I think it is more noteworthy for its omissions than for what it does. I think the most significant omission is with respect to the lack of provisions relating to the citizenship of children of Canadian citizens born outside Canada. Again I venture to draw to the attention of the parliamentary secretary Bill No. C-2 which I introduced and which has been commented upon favourably by literally hundreds of persons in the armed forces and the diplomatic service. This bill deals with the question of children bom outside Canada.
As the committee knows, at the present time a child born outside of Canada of a member of Canada's armed forces or a member of the diplomatic or other public service or the representative or employee of a Canadian firm or organization serving or engaged outside Canada will lose his citizenship unless two things are done. The first is that the birth has to be registered at a Canadian office abroad within two years. Second, between the ages of 21 and 24 that person must file a declaration of retention of Canadian citizenship.
There are today many thousands of Canadians serving or engaged outside of Canada, and I believe there are many children born out of this country who are likely to lose their Canadian citizenship unwittingly. I think that to place the children of Canadian citizens who are serving their country abroad either in the armed forces or diplomatic service in a different category from children of Canadians serving or engaged at home is discriminatory and a genuine hardship both to parents and children. I have had many descriptions of such hardship from members of the diplomatic service and armed forces who have told me that child No. 1 was born in Canada, that child No. 2 was born outside of Canada, that child No. 3 was born in Canada, that child No. 4 was bom outside of Canada, and so on. Some of these children have one type of status as Canadian citizens and others a different status. I just do not believe that this is good enough.
When we come to the question of the repeal of section 18, Mr. Chairman, I may have something further to say about the grounds of discrimination because I do not think that in this particular the government has gone far enough.

I should like to speak for a moment or two about the citizenship appeal court. The provision for appeal is, of course, an advance, but I wish that the Secretary of State had gone the full distance as did the Minister of Manpower and Immigration with respect to the immigration appeal board. What you will note here in respect to the citizenship appeal court, sir, is that there is no interference whatever with the discretion vested in the minister. Therefore the principal problem, which is that of security, is not touched on by this bill.
The hon. member for Matapedia-Matane has spent agonizing hours, as I have, in dealing with these very difficult security cases which come before the minister. Personally I do not think the bill in its present form is adequate; it provides simply for an appeal from the court, leaving the final discretion to the minister. This is exactly the opposite of what was done with the immigration appeal board, and I venture to suggest that the model of the immigration appeal board should be incorporated in this bill.
I wish only to reiterate that I am sorry there is not in this bill that clarion call to pride in Canadianism that I think there ought to have been today, five days before our confederation celebration. What I do not understand is why Canadian history and tradition are so badly taught in this country. Why are they not taught with that sense of drama and colour that I believe is so important in creating a genuine nation? Why do we as Canadians undersell our own history? I venture to suggest that it is as exciting, as dramatic, as full of courage as is to be found anywhere in the world. The story of our explorers is far more noteworthy and inspirational than the similar story in the United States, Australia or other countries of the world.
What we are not doing in this country is getting this story across to our younger generation. We are not teaching our youngsters to take a real, genuine pride in citizenship. I do not speak of chauvinism; I have no use for that. But I do believe in love for the soil of the nation, and this is what I think we should get across.
Recently I had a conversation with one of the senior ambassadors to Canada, and perhaps I am identifying him when I say that he knows Canada better than most Canadians. After all his travels around the world and across Canada he came to this conclusion. He said that if the full, exciting, dramatic story of Canada were told in all its colour, it would go further than anything to explain the

French to the English, each to the other, and Canada to the world. That, sir, is the type of clarion call that I think should be contained within the bill. That is the type of pride in our nationhood that I hope we can express on the first of July, one hundred years after our confederation.

Under present law, once an individual becomes a citizen it is not easy, and surely not desirable either, to take away that status or to revoke the passport. Hon. members do not need to have had very much experience in public affairs in the last few years to have some awareness of the benefits which an unscrupulous individual may gain from carrying a valid Canadian passport. We do not like the idea of revoking citizenship once granted. As will be seen from the provisions of this bill, citizenship will not be able to be revoked except in cases of fraud. The minister must decide whether this individual shall have that magic weapon put into his or her hands, a valid Canadian passport, which is granted along with Canadian citizenship. In every such case the eligibility of the person for citizenship is examined minutely on its own merits in the light of that intelligence.

I am also an authorized agent for the French National Railroads, Canadian National and Pacific railroads; the Travelers Insurance Company, Hartford, Connecticut, TJ.S.A., and sales representative for the Dominion Automobile Association. At the present time I am operating my business successfully, in the good consideration of the population of both cities.
I am a member of the St. Dominic Catholic Church and the Society Principe di Piemonte.
From the CFPA radio station I broadcast a weekly program and take active part in social and sport associations such as the Y.M.C.A. and soccer club.
I have never been charged or convicted of any offence, except for a couple of parking tickets.
I am married with a child and live in the respect of the people obeying in full the Canadian law.
The only crime, if crime it can be called, was when in 1953 following a period of long working hours and study of the English language, I consulted a doctor who advised me to be recovered in the Ontario Hospital.
I understand mine has been considered a mental case. In my opinion it was only a little ''esaurimento nervoso" if you forgive my use of this Italian expression. What I needed was some rest and as soon as I had it I got well.
My activities in these last ten years can speak for themselves and my employers can corroborate it.
Mr. Badanai, the reason I am detailing all this is to draw a picture of myself so that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration would see in the daylight the man against whom an order of deportation was issued.
Did I do anything wrong which is considered against the law in Canada? Are people allowed to get sick wherever they are? Now I admit I got sick, and without any arguing in regard to the diagnosis of my sickness, under any .law of any country I suppose it has been a natural thing which could have happened to anyone, Canadian or not Canadian.
Did I ever before and after my confinement in the hospital show any sign of insanity by acting

as a mental case? My life's record does not show any of that.
I have been living in Canada for the past 13 years and have always tried to be a good citizen, governing myself according to the Canadian law. I like this country, the way of living, the people, the law; I enjoy every bit of the Canadian freedom and I feel and consider myself a new Canadian.
What I am asking is to be officially recognized as such, so I do not have to feel as being one man too many in Canada, waiting to be sent away without, pardon me, any good reason.
Shall I just wait to be deported or continue my activities as a good Canadian citizen? I have a family, I own property and feel ashamed not being able to be considered a man with a right to vote and take an active part as a Canadian citizen in political life.
If the department considers that I am not a good man, an insane man, I would ask the minister to act accordingly in my regard. But if you, Mr. Badanai, and the minister of citizenship and immigration would consider a review of my case, cancel the order of deportation and grant me the citizenship of this country, I am willing and ready to assume officially the full responsibility of a good Canadian citizen.
It is a long letter and I am grateful to hon. members for allowing me to read it all and for listening to it. But I think it was worth while reading because this is not the only case of its kind. There are others. Many forms of mental illness appear now to be as curable as are certain types of physical ailments. The present Immigration Act was formulated before these important advances in medical knowledge were achieved and it is widely considered that the provisions of section 5 in relation to previous insanity are altogether unrealistic.
It seems to me that the scope of this bill should be increased so as to include a clause which would take care of specific cases such as the one I have just cited. Epilepsy is another affliction which has responded favourably to new treatments and medical techniques. Indeed, modern drugs may so control the disease that afflicted persons may suffer few, if any, symptoms, and live quite normal lives. I would like to have dealt with both these afflictions, insanity and epilepsy, at greater length but I do not wish to take advantage unduly of the indulgence of the committee. It is true that in many cases sufferers are allowed to remain in this country, but there is no way in which they can acquire Canadian citizenship.
Notwithstanding the shortcomings of this bill I am very happy to support it. I do feel, however, that the minister should seek to change the legislation so as to deal with the particular aspect I have drawn to his attention and bring its provisions into conformity

Mr. Chairman, I listened as carefully as I could to the statement made by the Secretary of State in connection with the amendment recently disposed of by the committee. She gave me at least the impression that the only occasion on which the minister would exercise the power of discretion would be when either the security of the state or criminal activity was involved. If this is indeed the case, and if its the hon. lady's view that this is the ground upon which previous ministers have acted, then it seems to me we are reaching the point at which, for practical purposes at least, the grounds for the rejection of applications for citizenship are being clarified and defined. But this is not what the legislation says. As it stands, the law gives unlimited power of discretion to the minister to reject an application on any ground as may appear to be desirable or necessary from time to time.
I must say I have had no occasion to approach the present minister in connection with any case in which an application for citizenship has been refused. But I think most hon. members over a period of years have had cases brought to their attention in which applications have been rejected for unknown reasons. These were cases in which by no stretch of the imagination, since the applicants were well known in the communities where they lived, was it possible to see how either the security of the state or criminal activity could enter into the picture. It occurs to me that the minister, by virtue of the position she is now taking, is herself suggesting in effect that the procedure which was established in connection with the immigration appeal board is one that could be considered in these circumstances. In other words, it should be clearly understood that one or other of these grounds applies. The minister has virtually said so. She has said that these are the only grounds which she will consider for rejection. This means that as long as she remains in her present portfolio an application will not be rejected except for one or other of these reasons. If this is going to be the basis of administration then it seems to me desirable that it should be the basis of the law so that people will know why they are being rejected.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
This may be the case so far as the applications with which the minister has dealt are concerned, but I have a vivid recollection of a
Canadian Citizenship Act case which happened quite a number of years ago. It involved a young married woman from what is now Yugoslavia before that country became Yugoslavia. Her husband preceded her to Canada. Later she found herself in the position that her husband was a naturalized citizen, all but one of her children were born in Canada, she herself was the grandmother of Canadians, but for some reason she was the only member of her family who could not become a citizen. That case puzzled hon. members and unless my judgment was wrong it puzzled the woman in question. This kind of situation should not be repeated and perpetuated.
The minister's statement, apart from some minor variations, was the same as statements I have listened to ad nauseam from ministers holding that portfolio since I first entered the house quite a number of years ago. It is a portfolio that has had many ministers in charge of it. Some former ministers have admitted to me that it is a thankless task in some aspects, and that may be one of the reasons why there have been so many ministers over the years.
A former minister, the hon. member for Carleton, indicated that he hoped to implement some changes. In view of the fact that the present minister was not prepared to accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Broadview, I ask her to consider redefining this discretionary power so that it will be understood it will only be exercised in respect of the reasons which she has said this afternoon would justify withholding citizenship from a legally landed immigrant who has met the residence qualifications.
We have heard it repeated time and time again that citizenship is a privilege and not a right. But those of us who are natural born citizens are increasingly coming to question whether this concept is one that should be perpetuated forever. We are coming to believe that a legally admitted landed immigrant who has been in this country a reasonable period of time should acquire the right to become a citizen.

I should like to come back to the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I do not feel that any person who comes to this country has the inalienable right to claim citizenship. If a person coming to this country has that right, then I as a Canadian have the right to go to another country and claim the right of citizenship there. There must be reciprocity; there must be the right of the individual. What the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is doing is asserting the right of an individual to citizenship in the country of his choice. If this is valid in the case of some person who is a native of another land, that is, that he can come to Canada and assert his right to citizenship in Canada, then it is my inalienable right as an individual in the same way to move to another country and claim the right of citizenship in that country.

I suggest that the hon. member should think about this situation a little more deeply. He is asserting the right of the individual to citizenship on behalf of the stranger who is admitted to this country as a landed immigrant. I have a great deal of sympathy for the right of the individual, but it is the right of Canada and the right of Canadians to say to strangers; "We will admit you; we will admit

I would not say to the government of the home land of any individual that I have the absolute right to determine whether I shall be admitted as an immigrant to that land and whether I shall be admitted to the rights of citizenship. It is not for me to say. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.
If we should go further, however, I would say that once we have granted the right of citizenship it cannot be removed except in the most exceptional cases. I can conceive of the case of an individual who seeks the haven of Canadian citizenship and then goes off to another land. For all practical purposes he has abandoned Canadian citizenship, or perhaps he has returned to his original land and has abandoned it. I believe this is part of the responsibility of citizenship. After all, it is not only up to the state to protect the status of citizenship. It is up to the individual to protect his own citizenship and that includes compliance with the reasonable requirements of citizenship in Canada or in any other land.
We are dealing with Canadian citizenship. It is within the rights of the Canadian nation to say, "We are accepting you as Canadian citizens but there are certain responsibilities therewith and one of them is that it is your duty to protect the right of citizenship." I would limit revocation to the most exceptional cases. If there were to be revocation, it would have to be on the basis of clearcut evidence of overt acts on the part of the individual concerned. There must be something which flows from it.
One might say to a person if he becomes a Canadian citizen, having been born a citizen of another land, that if he should leave Canada for ten years, fail to report back, fail to reside again in Canada, or fail to register he will lose his Canadian citizenship. This, I believe, is what the act now provides. There would be, however, certain involuntary conditions which might be involved. One would be incarceration in another country for political offences where there really is no guilt. Another would be the question of poverty or illness and therefore the inability to return. True enough, one might say that a person could register at a Canadian consulate abroad. However, human nature being what it is I would say that it must involve much more than mere neglect. It would require an overt act on the part of the individual if he were to be deprived of his Canadian citizenship.

Mr. Chairman, I have been prompted to take part in this interesting discussion because I heartily support the hon. member for Carleton's view that citizenship should be granted in many cases to those persons who have been denied citizenship because of their political beliefs. These persons would be entitled by our laws to sit in this house if they could get elected. I know of numerous cases of this type, although the number has been decreasing as the years go by. I know of persons with long residence in Canada who belong to certain groups, but because of gossip and certain information which has been spread they have been denied Canadian citizenship. In some cases they have even served in the defence of this country. I give the government credit because these matters are being reviewed from time to time and there has been improvement as the years have gone by.
I have listened carefully to the very interesting discussion that has been taking place and I should like to refer to something that happened in 1954 regarding my opposition to the granting of unlimited powers to the minister not only to keep people out but to bring people in against the advice of the immigration board. Let me quote a few lines in this respect, and this is a little difficult because I must quote myself from Hansard of June 26, 1954. At that time I was dealing with the case of five individuals who had been residents of Canada for six years. At that time they applied for citizenship and I had been informed that the board had ruled against their applications. As recorded at page 6808 of Hansard for June 26 of that year I said:
Earlier in the session the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked certain questions in the house-
The then hon. member for Winnipeg North wanted to know about certain French nationals who had arrived in Canada as landed immigrants and had been in this country for six years. The questions were answered and the answers indicated that some of them had been guilty of murder and had been sentenced by French courts. In this regard I had this to say:
In view of the law we cannot understand how these people were permitted to stay in Canada and how they were granted Canadian citizenship. We have in our possession copies of the judgments of the French courts, which were sent to us from

Paris. I am not reading the judgments, but I am going to read a couple of lines with respect to the sentences in each case.
Mr. Harris, the minister of citizenship and immigration at that time asked which case it was. I went on to state:
In fairness, Mr. Chairman, as I mentioned before,
I do not want to give the names. I will send the minister my slip when I am through.
This is what I read, and I will give one or two examples. In one case the individual was sentenced to death in absentia while he was in Canada, for dealing in time of war with a foreign power with a view to encourage that power against France. That was Inspector Waffen of the S.S., a branch of the Gestapo. In another case the individual was sentenced to death and the forfeiture of all his property for treason.
At that time the French ambassador was very disturbed about the matter and went to visit the minister and other members of the cabinet. He also came to see some members of this group and presented these documents from the French courts which clearly proved that these men, having committed murder and assisted the German state against the state of France during time of war, entered Canada under false names with false passports and were provided with false visas. As recorded on the same page I had this to say:
I might say that a high French government official stated they belonged to an organization who murdered the French minister, Georges Mandel, in the forest of Fontainebleau, massacred resisters, and betrayed allied parachutists who were hidden by brave Frenchmen who were shot. Some of these parachutists may have been some of our own men.
Regardless of this evidence these men were granted citizenship. This is another danger in giving unlimited responsibility to the minister in relation to granting citizenship under certain circumstances. Can anyone say why these men, who had been landed immigrants for six years, were entitled to Canadian citizenship? Certainly they were not because they had entered Canada with false documents and were proven by evidence and French court documents to have been guilty of various crimes and sentenced to death or life imprisonment. This is one objection I have to putting unlimited responsibility in the hands of the minister, not only in respect of keeping people out but also under certain circumstances of letting them in against the advice provided by responsible authorities. I have a great deal of correspondence regarding these cases in my office, but I do not intend to deal with it further at this time. This information came
June 27, 1967	COMMONS
from the French ambassador who was highly indignant about the situation.
We must be very careful in these matters, and I am more inclined to delve into the character of these people than the skills they may possess. I know of a chap who came here in 1956. He was a criminal in the country from which he came. He moved to the interior of British Columbia and it was not long before he committed another offence and was jailed. I went into this matter very carefully with other persons who had been associated with him and it turned out he was a very poor character indeed. Could anyone say that this man, after having been sentenced to jail in this country, should be entitled to Canadian citizenship? I was told not long ago that he was back in jail again. Would he have any right to Canadian citizenship? That man is a Canadian citizen today.
I took this matter up with the minister at the time and he said there was an agreement not to send persons back behind the Iron Curtain. I should like to know with whom that agreement was made because if I had anything to do with that type of man he would have been sent back long ago.
We are very fortunate in our part of the country in having an excellent county court judge who goes through these applications and records very carefully. I know of another individual who came here as an immigrant with a criminal record. Less than a year ago he applied to the county court judge for citizenship but was rejected on the basis of evidence provided by the chief of the Nelson city police. That man had been in quite a bit of trouble and it was very fortunate that his application was rejected. At the present time he is in penitentiary.
I know of another chap who arrived here six months ago on an assisted passage from a country in Europe. He had only been in the Kootenays for five months when he visited a doctor friend of mine, pulled out a long knife and stabbed him five times. It was only because of the courage of the doctor's female secretary that he escaped when she jumped on top of this assailant. This man was sent to a mental hospital from which he escaped quite recently. The police have had to place a guard on the doctor because the man is mentally deranged. The latest information I have is that he left Vancouver on a Spanish ship and I suppose has gone back to where he came from. We are "out" the amount of the assisted passage.

Personally, I value more highly a person being of good character than his lacking a few skills. I believe we must be more careful in some cases than we have been in the past. Mr. Chairman, I did not raise this point when I spoke earlier in the debate because I feel this clause is almost an omnibus one covering a number of different areas. I want to draw the attention of the committee to what appears to me to be a conflict in drafting between the amended section 31, which is the last portion of clause 7 of the bill before us, and amended section 12 which is referred to in clause 3 of the bill.
When you look at the citizenship act itself, part II, you see that section 10 (1) provides that if a person satisfies the citizenship court of certain matters, his knowledge of English, that he is of good character, is a fit and proper person to be a Canadian citizen, and so on, the minister may grant a certificate of ciizenship. Section 12, which is referred to in clause 3 of the bill and is found in part II of the act, provides:
A certificate of citizenship granted to any person under this part, other than to a minor under the age of 14 years, shall not take effect unless that person has taken the oath of allegiance set forth in the second schedule, and that person shall become a Canadian citizen upon the granting to him of the certificate of citizenship or on his taking the oath of allegiance, whichever later occurs.
If you look at part VI of the act, under the heading "Procedure and Evidence" it gives the procedure to be followed by the court in considering the application of a person for Canadian citizenship under section 10 (1).
June 27, 1967

However, section 31, which is one of the concluding portions of part VI headed "Procedure and Evidence" and is amended by the bill before us, provides in the last part:
-a certificate of citizenship may, in the discretion of the minister, be granted to the applicant and the certificate shall be delivered to the applicant and the oath of allegiance taken by him as prescribed by regulation.
It would seem to me there is some kind of conflict here. Section 12, to which I have referred, seems to call rather specifically for the person granted the certificate to take a specific oath in a specific form referred to in a schedule to the act before he can become a citizen. Section 31, in the last portion of clause 7 which we are about to dispose of, would appear to say that an oath of allegiance is to be taken under exactly the same circumstances but it can be prescribed by regulation.

However, I feel it should be dealt with, particularly since the minister in answer to a question of mine said that in spite of the seemingly specific requirement that a person becoming a citizen must swear allegiance through an oath to the crown and the country he can affirm if the taking of the oath is against his religious beliefs. The basis of that answer was an opinion given by the Department of Justice.
I realize there are various procedural inhibitions with respect to references in this house to the exact terms of an opinion by the Department of Justice. Mr. Chairman, I have but one rather short comment to make on the exchange which took place a few moments ago between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I found it fantastic that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should ask the hon. member for Edmonton West: Why is there a difference between a native-born Canadian citizen and a Canadian naturalized under the Immigration Act?
That is self-evident. Such a question is so naive that it is almost incomprehensible, for after all, Mr. Chairman, there are natural laws against which nothing can be done. Take for example the case of a son or daughter of a family, born in that family, a natural child-in the non-pejorative sense of the word-who has ties of blood with his parents and natural rights which do not need to be conferred upon him. Suppose that, in the same family, the father and mother decide to adopt a child. The adopted child may enjoy the same privileges as the other children, because they have been granted him, because he benefits from the privileges of the sons born to that family. Nonetheless, there will be no ties of blood in the second case, and the adopted child will only become a member of the family through the generosity of the parents! who decided to adopt him.
It is the same thing, I think, for an immigrant who wants to become a Canadian citizen. If the country decides to grant him the favour of adopting him then, I think, he will be given the same privileges as others, but until the title of Canadian citizen has been granted to him, until he has taken the oath required in the circumstances, he is not entitled to demand it. It is a gift. But those who were born in this country have a natural right, they are natural members of the family, they are kith and kin, and nothing holds
June 27, 1967

against that. That is natural law, Mr. Chairman.
That is why I find fantastic the claim of those who say that immigrants coming here should have the right to demand Canadian citizenship, to be treated like the others. I do not think it is reasonable to ask this. They are already given much by being accepted and adopted here in the country, so let them meet the conditions.

Mr. Chairman, may I commend the committee on the rapid progress it has made. May I thank the hon. member for his words of welcome. I hope that the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria will be equally commendatory when I have finished my statement.
On June 22 the Prime Minister undertook that a statement would be made this week on steel producing operations in the Sydney area of Cape Breton. We have been giving this matter consideration for some time because we realize the importance of this industry to the local economy.
It would appear that the problem in Sydney arises from a number of factors, including some softening in the market not only in Canada but in most countries for some of the kinds of steel which Dosco Steel Limited produces. Because the Sydney plant is at a considerable distance from the main Canadian markets for steel, the company faces keen competition from most other domestic producers who are closer to these markets. The company reports that it has been rationalizing its operations in order to improve its ability to meet increased competition from Canadian
June 27, 1967	COMMONS
and other producers, and this also has affected the situation.
Furthermore, faced with increasing competition and declining prices in its main marketing areas the company says it has taken steps to improve the productivity of its operations at Sydney which have resulted in some curtailment of the numbers employed.
In addition, there is a world-wide overcapacity of steelmaking facilities, and imports of certain steel products into the areas of Canada which are readily accessible by sea have been increasing. These areas are also the main markets in which products made from Sydney steel are sold. It has been said by Dosco that some of the imports may involve dumping and the Department of National Revenue has been asked to undertake an appropriate investigation as quickly as possible.
It is evident from these facts that the problem in Sydney relates not only to general market factors, but equally it relates to special problems for this company. In these circumstances, the government has come to the view that stockpiling of Sydney steel does not provide a solution to either of these problems. Moreover it would not be an appropriate measure for the federal government to initiate in these circumstances.
We do not believe, however, that there is a long term general problem in Canada affecting the steel industry as a whole. Rather, the problems affecting the steel operations in Sydney, although aggravated by the current market situation, appear to be of a special nature.
Because of the complexity of the problem it would seem to me that if a thorough study of the steel industry in Cape Breton were available, this would make it easier for the responsible authorities to examine the problem in a more informed way.
It is of course recognized that the government of Nova Scotia has the prime responsibility for the special problems of industry within that province, but if it were the wish of the government of Nova Scotia to undertake a study with respect to the steel industry the Department of Industry would be ready to co-operate. In fact the government of Nova Scotia, working in co-operation with various federal departments and agencies and the company, has already done some work in this field.
I should report, Mr. Chairman, that a number of federal activities have already helped to bring new industries to Cape Breton. Under the federal area development program, 27053-129

Cape Breton Development Corporation applications have been approved involving new investment in manufacturing industry of some $132 million. These facilities will create new jobs in Cape Breton. I have not been a member of this house long, Mr. Chairman, but I have been in political activities for a long time, and since the 1930's I do not recall such callous disregard of a problem that kicks the government in the teeth, and it refuses to do anything about it. If stockpiling steel is not reasonable or practicable, then come up with some other solution, make some other suggestion that will solve the problem. But instead of that there is a long string of excuses for the situation, ending up in the suggestion that a study be made.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria said he welcomed this study, and of course I welcome it too. Studies are always useful if one learns more; but I say there is no need for any further study now. The area of Cape Breton has been studied to distraction. There have been studies upon studies upon studies in the last three decades, and if the government does not yet know what the problem is in Cape Breton, no new study will enlighten it.
The problem of the Sydney steel plant is not terribly difficult even for the layman to understand. The simple proposition is that Dosco and the Hawker Siddeley group have decided that from the point of view of the profitability of the corporation it is more profitable to build a steel complex in Con-trecoeur, 40 miles from Montreal, than to modernize the plant at Sydney. It is just as simple as that. So they have gradually taken away parts of the operation in the Sydney plant to Contrecoeur, and threaten to take
Cape Breton Development Corporation away even the basic steel production from Sydney to Contrecoeur within a few years.
Obviously if they are going to have all the secondary and processing plants at Contrecoeur, it will be a great deal cheaper and more economical for the corporation to have the production of basic steel located where the manufacturing and processing operations are carried on. This is what faces this government, the government of Nova Scotia and the people of Cape Breton.
Over the past decade there has been, not a gradual but a precipitous reduction in the operations of the steel plant at Sydney. Despite the promises made by the heads of Dosco and A. V. Roe, to which the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria referred, the fact is that they have ignored the needs of Cape Breton. They are like all corporations. I am not blaming the corporation. They are not in Cape Breton for philanthropic purposes. They went there in order to build an industry that was going to pay them dividends and profits, and when the industry could not do so they moved elsewhere.
I am not blaming the corporation at all; but I am blaming the government in the strongest possible language for its lack of courage, lack of vision and of a simple sense of public responsibility in replying to this dire, serious situation by saying, "There will be no stockpiling. There will be another study so that we can have another volume to put on some shelf or under some desk."
There was the statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare just one month ago today, on May 27, that because of certain things done the outlook for employment was going to improve. But now his government sits here, with a thousand more people off work than there were a month ago, and there is not a single suggestion of what should be done. This brings me back to what I have said on two or three occasions, and what other hon. gentlemen have supported.
The situation in Cape Breton steel means that the government should have taken over the steel plant as well as the coal mining operations on that island, because there is no other way in which the economic problem of that island can be solved, or can even be attacked intelligently. Why is the government ready to take over the coal operation? It is because over a long number of years Dosco has been reducing coal production, threatening to stop it completely and get out because of the uneconomic character of those operations. For years the federal government has

Cape Breton Development Corporation paid subventions-and I am not being critical of that at all-in order to maintain the industry at some level. But despite those subventions the industry kept going down and so, following the Dr. Donald report, the government has decided to take over the coal operations.
Exactly how long do the people of Cape Breton have to suffer before this self-righteous, absolutely callous government realizes that action has to be taken because precisely the same thing has happened with steel as has happened with coal? The operations are reducing week by week, month by month, year by year; men are being thrown out in the street, and women too from the offices of the company. There is no hope whatever that this company will do anything to modernize, rationalize and diversify its steel operation in Sydney. These are the only solutions-to modernize, to rationalize and to diversify, or to introduce the production of construction steel, as advocated by experts, particularly the standard sizes, designs and forms of construction steel for use in the Atlantic provinces and for export, particularly to the new nations of the world which have a great demand for that kind of product.

INDUSTRY-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR CANADIAN FILM PROCESSORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for keeping the minister a little later on this late, late show, but my remarks will take only a few moments. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister something about which he may not be aware, and which I think is very important.
There is currently being distributed throughout Canada a promotional envelope soliciting photo-finishing at American mail order prices. The address to which the films are to be mailed for processing is the capital of the film world, Hollywood, California, U.S.A. The prices advertised are considerably lower than Canadian prices for similar processing. This in itself is all right. There is nothing wrong with competition in business as long as it is fair competition. But the question here is whether this is fair competition.
If we look at the facts we see first that the processing procedures for film are fairly well standardized in the United States and Canada. The equipment is identical in most instances. However, Canadian film processors in the photographic industry obtain most of their equipment from the United States. This is also true of photographic chemicals and other supplies of that nature entering this country. And here we have the first snag: Present government policy dictates that Canadian film processors must pay duty on all equipment, chemicals and supplies entering this country. Thus the cost of all photographic supplies in Canada is much higher than in the United States largely due to our Canadian duties and taxes.
In addition, still looking at the facts, Canadian processors add to the general economy of the country, as the minister knows, by paying income taxes and other taxes incidental to their Canadian citizenship. About this they do not complain unduly, since they are as willing as any other Canadians to undertake their obligations of citizenship. However, when they see competition from the United States threatening their livelihood because of arbitrary decision by government, or government directive, they are understandably disturbed.
What is this arbitrary, bureaucratic directive? It is that although Canadian processors must pay taxes and duty, instead of helping them by lowering these taxes and duties the government has seen fit to try the hands
June 27, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion across the border routine, and has permitted Canadian photo processing to be done in the United States and returned to this country duty free. I would submit to the minister that this is discrimination. Perhaps the minister is not aware that this sort of thing is going on. Certainly our American friends are aware of the situation and have been quick to seize on the excellent business afforded by our centennial year and by Expo, and have not hesitated to exploit the Canadian photo processing business for their own monetary advantage.
The industry is not asking for any special favour, but only for fair treatment. Either duty should be charged on the incoming processed film, or the photographic equipment, chemicals and other supplies used by our photographic industry should be duty free on entering this country. After all, our labour costs are somewhat lower here than they are in Hollywood and our industry could compete favourably with the United States industry if some of these arbitrary barriers to such competition were removed.
I would ask the minister to consider doing something about this. As he knows, this is a seasonal business, mainly conducted in the summer months. It is very important to our photo processors that something be done to help them in what is certainly their time of need. It does not help when they see envelopes like the one I now hold in my hand coming from Hollywood with the Canadian centennial emblem on them, giving a quasiofficial stamp of Canadian approval to this method of soliciting business. I am sure the minister does not approve of this. Perhaps he will have some way to relieve this undue or unfair competition to the Canadian photo processing industry.

maintopic: INDUSTRY-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR CANADIAN FILM PROCESSORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue has asked me to answer this question for him tonight, and so I regret the disappointment occasioned the hon. member for Saskatoon. However, I hope the information I have for him will be acceptable.
In answering the question I should first point out that the importations of which he speaks are not commercial importations, but are importations made by individual amateur photographers which consist of film exposed by them while abroad or at home in Canada. Much of this film was purchased by them at "process included" prices and returned for processing to the film manufacturer's processing plant.

An exposed or processed film has for years been considered as being of no commercial value when imported for personal use and not for resale. Over the last year or so film processors in Canada have expressed views similar to those expressed by the hon. member. As a result, investigations were made to establish the validity of their claims. At that time little or no evidentiary support was available to uphold these claims or warrant a change in the non-commercial classification given to processed film imported by individuals for personal use and not for resale.
[DOT] (11:20 p.m.)
Recently the department entered into consultation with the Department of the Registrar General, who had requested that consideration be given in this matter to the consumer interests involved. At present the two departments are studying the price structure and other characteristics of the industry, taking into consideration the representations of the industry as well as those of the consumers.
I am advised that the results of these joint discussions may be expected in the near future.

HOUSE OF COMMONS-APPLICATION TO STAFF OF BILINGUAL BONUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 6, 1966, the Prime Minister announced in the house his policy on bilingualism.
It will be recalled that these new methods of encouraging bilingualism will touch, in the first place, the positions requiring university training, second, executive and administrative positions and, finally, clerical and secretarial positions.
In the case of clerks and secretaries, a bonus will be paid in respect of clerical and secretarial positions in which there is a requirement for a knowledge of both official languages, provided the incumbents of such positions shall meet standards of competence established by the Public Service Commission.
In addition, the government was to take a certain number of general measures that would solidly establish bilingualism in the public service and in the federal capital.
This policy announced on April 6, 1966, Mr. Speaker, indicated and revealed a certain ment although, at the time, this policy seemed effort in the right direction by the govern-
June 27, 1967	COMMONS
quite timid and overly gradual, as emphasized to me by some members, by many newspaper commentators and by other Canadian citizens.
That policy, also set forth on April 6, contained certain deficiencies. Right then, a true statute of bilingualism should have been defined and the criteria whereby bilingualism fills a need should have been determined, rather than leaving the decision to the fancy of the new secretariat within the Privy Council. In addition, the creation of a protective and arbitration organization to settle grievances which would unavoidably arise was then overlooked.
It is to be wondered today, after this new policy on bilingualism has been in force for 15 months, exactly what progress has been made with regard to the positions then to be considered, first office clerks and secretaries, and also in the spirit that prompted the very statement of the Prime Minister, who was anxious to introduce bilingualism as soon as possible within the public service in the national capital. This measure seemed to be appropriate, in view of the following year, that is the present centennial year.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it seems now that this policy has not been followed according to the announcement then made. Apparently, a bonus of 7 per cent has been granted to certain classes of civil servants, that is to the clerks or secretaries, but according to some rumours, it seems that several of these classes have not yet benefited by this bonus for bilingual employees.
Naturally, there is some talk of not disturbing employees of long standing who are not bilingual and more or less interested in learning other languages. The point must be taken into consideration. Although we must not hurt employees of long standing who, particularly in the national capital, did not see the need of learning both of the official languages of Canada, believing the country to be unilingual, or thought it sufficient to speak only one language, we must also remember bilingual Canadians, found mostly and in great majority among the French Canadians.
I am proud to say that we French Canadians understood the bilingual and bicultural nature of our country, and that our contribution in this respect has been great, although a certain discrimination is practised against several thousand civil servants who are apparently bilingual and competent, and who do 10 per cent of their work in the other official Canadian language.

We should therefore like to know from the government to what extent that policy has been implemented, and just how far the secretariat set up within the Privy Council has progressed with its work.
May I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to ask the government not to let another hundred years go by, not to let another generation die, before implementing bilingualism somewhat intelligently and rapidly. Because most of the bilingual people are French Canadians, they should not continue to be discriminated against through slow implementation of the program.
That is why I wish to point out to the government how important it is to extend rapidly the bilingual standards advocated by the April 6 policy, to implement that policy in the federal capital, to extend the premium for bilingualism to the secretaries of the members, who are extremely competent, to the messengers, to the members of the parliament security service, to the employees of the various divisions of the house. I appeal, particularly, to the Speaker to kindly go along with this policy on bilingualism. We have bilingual constables. We would like to have more who would be able to answer the people who come here in the two official languages.
Several of the pages are bilingual as well and would deserve this bonus which is a token of competence and enrichment for any Canadian.
That is why we would also agree to an extension of bilingualism, and this bonus be granted to the employees of crown corporations, the armed forces, the R.C.M.P. and also the small wage-earners of the public service, just as in the case of government employees.
I am making this appeal because this is the best time to do so. By the way, July 1 and July 3 are not far away. July 3 is Confederation Day. It would be a good time to announce such a generous, liberal and Canadian policy.
